beginner: Limes care about drainage more than soil type. They grow well in sandy and even rocky ground as long as water never sits around the roots, since soggy soil brings on the foot rot in the disease notes. Deep, loose loam is ideal. On heavy clay, plant the tree high on a raised mound so water drains away. (Sources: UF/IFAS CH092, UF/IFAS CH093.)
seasoned: Limes are well adapted to a wide range of soils, including the deep sands and shallow calcareous rocklands of south Florida, but sharp drainage is non-negotiable: they do not tolerate flooded conditions, and wet feet drive Phytophthora foot rot. Deep, well-drained loam or sandy loam is ideal; slightly acidic is preferred, though limes tolerate high-pH calcareous soils if minor-element deficiencies are managed. Plant high on a raised mound on heavy or poorly drained ground. (Sources: UF/IFAS CH092, UF/IFAS CH093.)

beginner: Limes like slightly acidic soil (about pH 6.0 to 6.5) but grow in a wide range as long as drainage is good. In high-pH (alkaline) soil, plan to add iron and zinc so the leaves stay green.
seasoned: Limes prefer a slightly acidic soil around pH 6.0 to 6.5 but tolerate a broad range (roughly 5.5 to 8.0), including the alkaline calcareous soils of the Florida Keys and rockland. On high-pH ground, expect iron, manganese, and zinc to become less available and plan on nutritional foliar sprays and chelated iron rather than trying to acidify the whole site. (Sources: UF/IFAS CH092, UF/IFAS CH093.)

beginner: Feed from early spring through summer in small, regular doses, then stop by late summer. Feeding late in the year pushes out soft new growth that frost can damage, and limes are the citrus most easily hurt by cold. If your soil is alkaline, the tree will also need iron and zinc so its leaves stay green. Keep fertilizer off the trunk and water it in.
seasoned: Feed in light, frequent doses from late winter or early spring through summer, then taper by late summer so late flushes harden before any cold; feeding too late pushes tender growth into frost season, which a lime can least afford. Young trees take small amounts several times a year, building from a fraction of a pound to a few pounds annually as the tree matures. On the calcareous soils where limes are often grown, add nutritional sprays and chelated iron to head off minor-element deficiency. Keep fertilizer off the trunk and water it in.

beginner: Use a citrus fertilizer or one with plenty of nitrogen (the first number on the label). In alkaline (high-pH) soil, the tree also needs iron and zinc, often sold as chelated micronutrients, to keep the leaves green. Skip fertilizers heavy in phosphorus (the middle number).
seasoned: Nitrogen-forward; use a fertilizer formulated for citrus. Young citrus trees take a balanced citrus grade with part of the nitrogen from organic sources; bearing trees shift toward higher potassium and lower phosphorus. On alkaline or calcareous soils, supplement with chelated iron and nutritional sprays of manganese and zinc, and avoid phosphorus-heavy formulas, which worsen iron lockout.

beginner: Give smaller amounts several times a year rather than one big feeding, and feed more as the tree grows. The simplest path is a citrus fertilizer at the label rate for the tree's age. Scatter it under the branches, not against the trunk.
seasoned: Scale the annual nitrogen to tree age and size, splitting it into several light applications rather than one heavy dose. UF/IFAS suggests roughly a quarter pound of a young-tree fertilizer at planting, working up to a few pounds per tree annually over the first several years. Spread feed evenly under the canopy and keep it off the trunk.

beginner: Keep grass and weeds away from under a lime tree, out to the edge of the branches. They steal water and food the tree needs, and a trimmer used against the trunk can wound the bark. Keep mulch a hand's width back from the trunk. You do not need a second tree for it to fruit.
seasoned: For a tree, companions really means root-zone management, not vegetable pairing. Keep lawn grass and weeds cleared out to the drip line: turf competes hard for water and nitrogen and slows a young lime, and string trimmers used to fight grass at the trunk nick the tender bark. Keep organic mulch pulled back at least a foot from the trunk to reduce Phytophthora foot-rot risk. Limes are self-fruitful, so no second tree is needed for pollination. UF/IFAS also cautions against heavy lawn fertilization and herbicide drift near citrus. Low, shallow-rooted plantings well outside the drip line are harmless; anything crowding the trunk or holding moisture against it is not. (Sources: UF/IFAS CH092, Texas A&M AgriLife.)

beginner: Keep lawn grass from growing right up to your lime tree. Grass competes with citrus for water and nutrients, especially while the tree is young, flowering, and flushing. Mowing and trimming close to the trunk can also nick the thin bark. Keep a clear or mulched circle around the base instead.
seasoned: Grass under the tree steals water and food a young lime needs, and trimming it against the trunk can wound the bark. Keep it cleared out to the edge of the branches.

beginner: Pull weeds away from the base of your lime tree. Weeds against the trunk steal water and nutrients, and they give cover to pests and rodents that gnaw the bark. Keep a weed-free or lightly mulched space around the trunk, with any mulch pulled back a little so it does not sit against the bark.
seasoned: Weeds and damp material crowding the trunk hold moisture against the bark and can rot the base. Keep the area right around the trunk clear and dry.

beginner: The Asian citrus psyllid is a small brown insect that feeds on new growth with its back end tilted up. By itself it does little harm, but it spreads citrus greening, a fatal disease. It is a real problem in Florida and parts of the Gulf, California, Texas, and Arizona, and absent from most of the country.
seasoned: Tiny mottled-brown insects that feed on young flush at a tail-up angle, leaving a characteristic white, waxy, ribbon-like excretion and twisted, notched new leaves. The psyllid itself does limited feeding damage; its importance is entirely as the vector of Huanglongbing (citrus greening). It is a serious concern in Florida and parts of the Gulf, California, Texas, and Arizona, and is absent or under quarantine in much of the rest of the country.

beginner: The psyllid carries the greening germ from a sick tree to a healthy one while feeding on new leaves. Moving citrus plants between areas spreads it, which is why some states restrict carrying citrus around.
seasoned: The psyllid (Diaphorina citri) picks up the greening bacterium from an infected tree and injects it into healthy flush as it feeds. Moving citrus plant material across regions spreads both insect and disease, which is why citrus is quarantined in affected states.

beginner: If you live where the psyllid is present, buy certified healthy trees, do not bring citrus in from other areas, and tell your local extension office if you think you see it. Elsewhere, just do not import citrus from quarantine areas.
seasoned: Only where ACP is present: buy certified disease-free trees, never move citrus material across quarantine lines, inspect new flush for psyllids, and report suspected finds to your county extension or agricultural commissioner. Where ACP is absent, simply do not import citrus from quarantined areas.

beginner: Spraying your own tree does little against the psyllid. What helps is spotting it early, reporting it, and removing a tree confirmed to have greening so it does not infect others.
seasoned: Backyard chemical control of ACP is of limited value and is best coordinated through regional area-wide programs, not tree by tree. The meaningful home action is early detection, reporting, and removing confirmed greening-infected trees to protect the area.

beginner: Leafminer makes shiny, squiggly trails inside new leaves, and the leaves curl and look distorted. On limes it is worth watching because the damage opens the door to citrus canker, a disease limes catch easily.
seasoned: Silvery, winding tunnels just under the surface of young leaves, which curl and twist around the larva's path. Damage tracks each flush of soft foliage in the warm months. On limes it matters more than on many citrus because the wounds it leaves are entry points for citrus canker, to which limes are highly susceptible; on mature trees the leaf injury itself is largely cosmetic.

beginner: A tiny moth lays eggs on brand-new leaves and the caterpillar tunnels inside. It can only attack soft new growth, not older tough leaves.
seasoned: The larva of a small moth (Phyllocnistis citrella) feeds between the surfaces of tender new leaves; it cannot mine hardened mature leaves, so damage follows each flush.

beginner: Do not over-fertilize or over-prune, which push out the tender new leaves the moth wants. Leave lightly mined leaves on the tree, since they still feed it. Keeping leafminer down also helps limit canker.
seasoned: Avoid heavy nitrogen and off-season pruning that push extra tender flush, so growth is synchronized and the vulnerable window is short. Do not strip mined leaves that are still green and working. Where canker is present, controlling leafminer also reduces canker entry wounds.

beginner: On an older tree, do nothing. On a young tree, coat the new growth with horticultural oil to discourage the moth, reapplying as fresh leaves appear. Avoid strong insecticides, which kill the helpful wasps.
seasoned: On mature trees, treatment is usually unnecessary. On young trees, a half-to-one-percent horticultural oil on emerging flush deters egg-laying and slows larvae; reapply as each new flush appears, since oil is short-lived. Avoid broad-spectrum insecticides, which kill the parasitic wasps that attack leafminer.

beginner: Aphids are tiny soft insects, often brown, green, or black, packed onto new leaves and buds so the growth curls up. You may also see stickiness, a black film, and ants.
seasoned: Clusters of soft green, brown, or black insects on new flush, flower buds, and the undersides of tender leaves, which curl and distort. Honeydew and black sooty mold often follow, along with ants. Aphids mainly trouble young trees and continuously flushing limes.

beginner: Aphids feed on the softest new growth. The brown citrus aphid can also carry a citrus virus, but spraying one tree does not stop that, so you treat only for the feeding damage.
seasoned: Several aphid species colonize new growth. The brown citrus aphid (Toxoptera citricida) is an efficient vector of citrus tristeza virus, though area-wide spread makes spraying a single backyard tree ineffective for virus prevention, so the reason to act is the feeding damage itself.

beginner: Do not over-fertilize, since lots of soft growth invites aphids. Most of the time you can leave them alone; ladybugs and other helpers clean them up as the leaves toughen.
seasoned: Avoid pushing excess tender flush with heavy nitrogen. Tolerate low numbers: ladybugs, lacewings, and parasitic wasps usually bring aphids under control within a few weeks as the flush hardens off.

beginner: Blast them off with a hose, or spray insecticidal soap if there are a lot. On an older tree you usually do not need to spray at all.
seasoned: A strong jet of water knocks colonies off tender shoots and is often enough. Insecticidal soap or horticultural oil handles heavier outbreaks on young trees; spraying an established tree is rarely warranted.

beginner: Scale shows up as tiny crusty or waxy bumps stuck to twigs, leaves, and fruit. They do not move, so they look like part of the bark. Some kinds leave the leaves sticky, and a black film (sooty mold) grows on the stickiness.
seasoned: Small, immobile bumps along stems, leaf midribs, and leaf undersides, and on fruit: armored scales (including Florida red scale and snow scale, both noted on limes) sit as hard discs, while soft scales are rounder and shinier. Soft scale and its honeydew bring sooty mold and ants. Heavy infestations cause yellow blotching, leaf drop, and twig dieback.

beginner: Scale are sap-sucking insects that build up fastest when ants are present, since ants chase off the helpful bugs that would eat them.
seasoned: Several armored and soft scale species suck sap from citrus. Populations build on crowded, dusty, or ant-tended trees, because ants protect scale from the predators and parasitic wasps that normally control it.

beginner: Keep ants out of the tree with a sticky band around the trunk so natural predators can do their job, and check any new tree for bumps before you plant it.
seasoned: Keep trees unstressed and not dusty, and control ant access to the canopy with a sticky trunk band so resident predators and parasites can work. Inspect new nursery stock, since scale often arrives on it.

beginner: Spray horticultural oil to coat the bumps, getting the undersides of leaves and the stems. Do not spray on a hot day (over about 95°F) or when the tree is dry and stressed, or it can burn the leaves.
seasoned: Horticultural oil smothers scale and is the standard backyard control; thorough coverage of stems and leaf undersides matters most. Do not spray oil above about 95°F or on a drought-stressed tree, as it can burn foliage. Repeat as new crawlers appear.

beginner: Mites are almost too small to see, but they leave leaves and fruit looking dusty, speckled, or bronzed, sometimes with fine webbing. They get worse when the tree is hot, dusty, and dry.
seasoned: Fine stippling, bronzing, or a dull silvered cast on leaves and fruit, sometimes with faint webbing. Citrus red mite is most active from about November through June; rust mites russet the peel. Mites worsen in hot, dusty, water-stressed conditions and after broad-spectrum sprays kill their predators.

beginner: Mites are tiny relatives of spiders that feed on leaves and fruit. Dust and a dry, stressed tree make them multiply.
seasoned: Several mite species feed by puncturing leaf and rind cells. Dust, drought stress, and the loss of predatory mites to broad-spectrum insecticides all favor outbreaks.

beginner: Water the tree properly and rinse dust off the leaves in dry weather. Avoid strong insecticides, which kill the good mites that eat the bad ones.
seasoned: Keep trees well watered and hose dust off foliage in dry spells. Preserve predatory mites by avoiding broad-spectrum insecticides, which trigger worse secondary mite flare-ups.

beginner: Spray the undersides of the leaves with water. For a bad case, use horticultural oil, but not on a hot day or a dry, stressed tree.
seasoned: A forceful water spray to the leaf undersides suppresses populations. Horticultural oil controls heavier infestations, with the same heat and drought-stress cautions as for scale.

beginner: Mealybugs look like little tufts of white cotton wedged where leaves meet stems and around the fruit. They leave the same stickiness and black film as aphids and scale.
seasoned: Soft, white, cottony masses tucked into leaf axils, fruit clusters, and the calyx end of fruit. Like soft scale and aphids, mealybugs produce honeydew, so sticky foliage and sooty mold are common. Heavy populations cause leaf yellowing and premature fruit drop.

beginner: Mealybugs are sap-suckers that hide in tight spots on the tree. Ants protect them, so ant control matters here too.
seasoned: Mealybugs are sap-feeders that shelter in protected crevices and on fruit. As with scale, ant tending shields them from natural enemies and lets populations grow.

beginner: Keep ants out of the tree and check new plants for cottony patches. Natural predators usually handle the rest.
seasoned: Control ants, inspect new plants, and avoid the dense, unpruned, dusty conditions mealybugs prefer. Resident predators and parasites usually keep backyard numbers low.

beginner: Dab or spray the cottony clumps with insecticidal soap or horticultural oil, and repeat, since their waxy coat sheds the spray.
seasoned: Spot-treat colonies with a cotton swab or a spray of insecticidal soap or horticultural oil, ensuring contact with the protected masses. Repeat, since the waxy coating sheds spray.

beginner: This water-mold disease shows as sticky gum oozing from the lower trunk, dark soft bark near the ground, and a tree that slowly yellows and thins. A key clue: the leaves wilt and yellow but do not perk up when you water, which means rot rather than dryness.
seasoned: Oozing gum on the lower trunk and crown, dark, water-soaked or peeling bark near the soil line, and a slow decline with yellowing, thinning canopy when feeder roots are attacked. A telling sign is foliage that wilts and yellows but does not recover after watering, which separates it from ordinary drought stress. Limes are susceptible, and infection can extend up onto scaffold branches.

beginner: The disease lives in the soil and spreads in standing water. It takes hold when the ground stays soggy, when soil or mulch is piled against the trunk, or when the graft union is buried. Overwatering young trees is the most common cause.
seasoned: Soil-dwelling Phytophthora species (water molds, not true fungi) release swimming spores under wet conditions that splash onto the trunk or reach roots in saturated soil. Poor drainage, soil or mulch piled against the trunk, a buried graft union, and overwatering, especially of young trees, drive it.

beginner: Prevention is mostly about planting. Set the tree high on a little mound, keep the graft union well above the soil, make sure water drains away fast, keep mulch a hand's width back from the trunk, and do not aim water at the base. This is the most important disease to prevent up front.
seasoned: Design it out at planting: set the tree high on a raised mound with the graft union well above the soil and mulch line, provide sharp drainage, keep mulch pulled back a foot from the trunk, and never water the crown directly. A foot-rot-resistant rootstock adds protection. UF/IFAS also advises against wounding the trunk with mowers or trimmers.

beginner: First fix the drainage or overwatering, or nothing else helps. For a gummy spot on the trunk, carefully cut the dark dead bark back to healthy bark and let it dry. A bad case in the roots is hard to cure, so prevention is what matters.
seasoned: Correct the water and soil problem first; recovery is impossible without it. For an active trunk canker, scrape dark diseased bark back to a margin of healthy greenish bark and let it dry; exposing a buried crown to air can halt spread. Severe root rot on an established tree is hard to reverse, which is why prevention carries the weight.

beginner: Canker makes raised, rough, corky spots with a yellow ring on leaves and fruit, and the tree may drop leaves and fruit early. It is a regulated disease found mainly in Florida and the Gulf, so most growers elsewhere do not have to worry about it. Limes catch it especially easily.
seasoned: Raised, corky, brown lesions on leaves, twigs, and fruit, each typically ringed by a yellow halo, often with defoliation, twig weakening, and blemished, dropping fruit. It is a regulated bacterial disease established in Florida and the Gulf region and not a concern in most other citrus areas. UF/IFAS notes Key lime is highly susceptible, so of all citrus, limes need canker taken most seriously where it occurs.

beginner: A bacterium spread by wind-blown rain, dirty tools, and moving infected plants. It gets in through tiny openings and wounds, and leafminer damage makes it worse. Warm, wet, windy weather helps it spread.
seasoned: The bacterium (Xanthomonas citri, syn. X. campestris pv. citri) is spread by wind-driven rain, contaminated tools, and movement of infected plant material; it enters through pores and wounds, and leafminer damage increases susceptibility. Warm, wet, windy weather drives outbreaks.

beginner: If you live where canker is present: handle the tree only when dry, clean your tools, keep leafminer down, and use a copper spray on new growth in the wet season. Do not carry citrus plants out of a quarantine area.
seasoned: Where canker is present: choose tolerant types where available, avoid working the tree when wet, disinfect pruning tools, manage leafminer to reduce entry wounds, and apply copper protectant sprays to new flush during the wet season. Never move citrus material out of a quarantined area.

beginner: There is no cure once a tree has it, so the focus is on preventing spread. Copper sprays slow it and removing badly infected parts helps. Follow your local rules if you are in an affected area.
seasoned: There is no cure for an infected tree; management is preventive and regulatory. Copper protectants reduce spread and removing heavily infected material limits inoculum. Follow local regulatory guidance in affected regions.

beginner: This one mainly hits Key limes. It blights the flower buds and shoot tips (which wither and die back), spots the leaves, and makes young fruit fall off, so you get fewer limes. Persian (Tahiti) limes do not get it, which is one reason many people grow them instead.
seasoned: A disease essentially specific to Key lime: it blights flower buds and blossoms (withertip), kills shoot tips, spots leaves, and causes young fruit to drop, cutting production. UF/IFAS states Key lime is highly susceptible while Tahiti (Persian) lime appears to be immune, so choosing Persian lime sidesteps this problem entirely.

beginner: A fungus that attacks Key lime flowers, shoot tips, and young fruit in warm, wet weather. Persian limes are not affected.
seasoned: The fungus Colletotrichum gloeosporioides infects Key lime blossoms, shoots, and young fruit, especially in warm, wet, humid weather. Persian lime appears to be immune.

beginner: For Key lime in a humid area, give it full sun and airflow, water the ground rather than the leaves, and do not over-fertilize. The easiest fix is to grow a Persian lime, which does not get this disease.
seasoned: For Key lime in humid regions, plant in full sun with good air movement, avoid wetting the foliage during irrigation, and avoid pushing excess tender growth with heavy nitrogen. The simplest prevention is to grow Persian lime instead, since it appears to be immune.

beginner: On a Key lime, a copper spray during flushing and bloom is the usual treatment, along with good airflow and sun. A Persian lime needs no treatment for this.
seasoned: Copper fungicide timed to protect flushes and bloom is the accepted control on Key lime where pressure warrants; sanitation and full-sun, airy siting are the foundation. No treatment is needed on Persian lime.

beginner: Greening causes blotchy yellow leaves (in an uneven pattern), corky yellow veins, dieback, and small lopsided fruit that stays green on one side and tastes bitter. There is no cure and it eventually kills the tree. It is carried by the Asian citrus psyllid and is a problem in Florida and parts of the Gulf, California, Texas, and Arizona, but most of the country does not have it.
seasoned: Asymmetric blotchy yellow mottling that crosses leaf veins unevenly, corky yellow veins, twig dieback, and small, lopsided, poorly colored, bitter fruit with aborted seeds. Decline is progressive and ultimately fatal. UF/IFAS notes Key lime appears moderately tolerant, but the tree still declines and there is no cure. It is spread by the Asian citrus psyllid and is a regional concern in Florida and parts of the Gulf, California, Texas, and Arizona; it is absent from most of the country.

beginner: A bacterium spread by the Asian citrus psyllid (see the psyllid entry under pests) and by grafting from infected trees. Once a tree has it, it cannot be cured.
seasoned: A bacterium (Candidatus Liberibacter species) that colonizes the tree's vascular system, transmitted by the Asian citrus psyllid (see the ACP pest entry) and by grafting infected material. Once a tree is infected there is no recovery.

beginner: This only matters where the psyllid lives. There, buy certified healthy trees, help control the psyllid, check your tree often, and remove a tree that is confirmed infected. Elsewhere, just do not bring in citrus from affected areas.
seasoned: Only relevant where the psyllid and disease are present: buy certified disease-free trees, support area-wide psyllid control, inspect regularly, and promptly remove confirmed infected trees. Where ACP is absent, the safeguard is not importing citrus from affected regions.

beginner: There is no cure. The only real responses are controlling the psyllid, starting with healthy trees, and removing an infected tree.
seasoned: There is no treatment that cures HLB. Management is limited to vector control, clean stock, and removing infected trees. Research into tolerant varieties is ongoing but there is no home cure.

beginner: Greasy spot makes yellow blotches on top of the leaf and greasy dark patches underneath, and the tree drops those leaves early. It is mainly a humid-climate problem (Florida and the Gulf) in the rainy season, and dry-climate growers rarely see it.
seasoned: Yellow mottling on the upper leaf surface with corresponding greasy, brown to black blisters on the underside, leading to premature leaf drop, heaviest on the interior and lower canopy. It is primarily a warm, humid-region disease (Florida and the Gulf), most active in the rainy season from about May to September, and uncommon in arid citrus areas.

beginner: A fungus that grows on old fallen leaves and spreads in warm, wet, humid weather. Dry summers keep it from getting started.
seasoned: A fungus (Mycosphaerella citri) whose spores develop on decomposing fallen leaves and infect during warm, humid, wet weather. The long warm rainy season of the Southeast drives it; dry summers suppress it.

beginner: Rake up and toss fallen leaves, since the fungus grows on them, and keep the inside of the tree open to air. In humid areas a copper spray in early summer helps prevent it.
seasoned: Rake up and remove fallen leaves to cut the spore source, improve air movement through the canopy, and avoid overhead wetting. In high-pressure humid regions, one or two copper or copper-plus-oil sprays timed to early summer are the standard preventive.

beginner: A copper spray, sometimes with horticultural oil, is the usual treatment where it is a real problem, along with cleaning up fallen leaves. In a dry climate you usually do not need to treat it.
seasoned: Copper fungicide, alone or with horticultural oil, is the accepted control where pressure warrants; sanitation of fallen leaves remains the foundation. No treatment is generally needed in dry climates.

beginner: In warm, wet weather while the tree is flowering, the petals develop brown, water-soaked spots and then the tiny fruit drops off, leaving a little button on the branch. Because limes flower again and again through the rainy season, they are especially prone to it.
seasoned: Brown to orange, water-soaked lesions on flower petals during wet, humid bloom periods, after which the young fruitlets drop and a persistent button (the calyx and floral disc) is left behind on the twig. Because limes bloom repeatedly through warm, wet weather, they are particularly exposed to this crop-robbing disease.

beginner: A fungus that infects the open flowers in rainy, humid weather and makes the young fruit fall. It is worst during the rainy season when the tree is in bloom.
seasoned: The fungus Colletotrichum acutatum infects open flowers during rainy, humid conditions, causing the young fruit to abscise. The damage therefore lands only where wet weather and open bloom coincide.

beginner: Give the tree full sun and airflow, and do not wet the flowers with sprinklers while it is blooming. In wet climates a bloom-time fungicide may be needed. Avoid over-fertilizing, which pushes extra flowers into the wet weather.
seasoned: Plant in full sun with good air movement, avoid overhead watering during bloom, and where pressure is high, protect blooms with an appropriately timed fungicide during wet weather. Reducing continuous off-season bloom by not over-fertilizing helps limit exposed flowers.

beginner: A bloom-time fungicide during rainy weather is the treatment where this disease is common, along with full sun and airflow. Dry-climate growers rarely need to act.
seasoned: Copper or an appropriate fungicide timed to bloom during rainy spells is the control where the disease is established; cultural steps (full sun, airflow, no overhead wetting) reduce pressure. It is largely a humid-region concern.

beginner: Water deeply, then wait until the top inch or two of soil feels dry before watering again; do not keep the soil constantly wet. A new tree needs water every other day at first, then a couple times a week for the first months. An established tree in the ground needs water mainly during long dry spells. Check the soil with your finger instead of watering on a set schedule.
seasoned: Water deeply but let the top inch or two of soil dry between irrigations rather than keeping the root zone constantly wet. UF/IFAS suggests newly planted trees every other day for the first week, then once or twice a week for the first couple of months, tapering to watering only during prolonged dry spells for young trees and only during very prolonged dry periods for mature in-ground trees. Fast-draining sandy soils need more frequent attention. Let weather and soil, not a fixed calendar, drive timing.

beginner: When you water, give enough to soak the soil deeply through the whole root area, not just a splash on top. A good deep soak now and then beats a little water every day.
seasoned: Apply enough at each irrigation to wet the whole root zone to depth, then let it partially dry. Deep, thorough soakings encourage deep rooting; shallow, frequent sprinkles keep roots near the surface and leave the tree drought-prone.

beginner: Water the soil around the tree, not the trunk. A drip line or slow hose works well. Keep water, soil, and mulch pulled back from the trunk so the base stays dry. Try not to spray the flowers with sprinklers in humid weather, since that spreads disease.
seasoned: Water at the base of the tree and keep the trunk and crown dry; drip or a slow soaker around the drip line is ideal. Keep water, soil, and mulch off the trunk and graft union, since wet bark at the crown invites foot rot. Avoid overhead sprinklers during bloom, which favor postbloom fruit drop and greasy spot in humid climates.

beginner: If the leaves turn yellow and stay yellow even after you water, or the soil never seems to dry out, you are likely watering too much. Soggy soil leads to root rot. Let the top of the soil dry before watering again.
seasoned: Persistently yellowing leaves that do not recover after watering, leaf drop, and a declining canopy point to overwatering and the foot and root rot it enables. Constantly saturated soil and standing water near the trunk are warning signs in themselves; soil that never dries between waterings is the underlying problem. UF/IFAS warns that overwatering makes limes decline or grow unthrifty.

beginner: Leaves that wilt, curl, or look dull usually mean the tree is too dry, and it may drop flowers or little fruit when very thirsty. A quick droop on a very hot afternoon can be normal, but if watering does not perk it back up, look closer.
seasoned: Wilting or curling leaves, dull or cupped foliage, and, during stress, flower and young-fruit drop indicate the tree is too dry. Brief, recoverable midday wilt in extreme heat can be normal, but leaves that stay wilted after watering signal a watering problem rather than simple dryness.

beginner: A new lime needs water every other day at first, then a couple times a week for the first months. Soak deeply, then let the surface dry before watering again, and keep the trunk dry.
seasoned: UF/IFAS suggests watering a newly planted lime every other day the first week, then once or twice a week for the first couple of months, tapering as it establishes; fast-draining sandy soils need more. Soak deeply and let the top inch or two dry between waterings, and keep the trunk and graft union dry against foot rot.

beginner: The most important time to keep watering steady is from flowering through when the fruit fills out; big swings between dry and wet then make the tree drop flowers and fruit. Avoid sprinklers over the tree during bloom, and water at the base.
seasoned: Even soil moisture matters most from bloom through fruit set and sizing, the key time to irrigate a bearing lime (UF/IFAS): moisture swings here trigger flower and fruit drop. Avoid overhead sprinklers during bloom, which favor postbloom fruit drop and greasy spot in humid climates. Water at the base and keep it evenly moist.

beginner: The biggest watering mistake is keeping a lime too wet; too much water harms it more than too little. Soak deeply, let it dry a bit, then water again. An established tree in the ground needs water mainly during long dry spells.
seasoned: The most damaging mistake with limes is keeping the soil constantly wet, which UF/IFAS warns makes trees decline or grow unthrifty: water deeply and infrequently, letting the top inch or two dry. A mature in-ground lime needs water mainly during very prolonged dry spells. Let weather and soil drive timing.

beginner: The biggest watering mistake is keeping a lime too wet; too much water harms the tree more than too little. Soak deeply, let it dry a bit, then water again, and keep the trunk dry.
seasoned: The most damaging watering mistake with limes is keeping the soil constantly wet, which causes more tree loss than underwatering. Aim for deep soak, partial dry, repeat, and always keep the trunk and graft union dry.

render_evidence: no renderer; watering is in herb FACT_KEYS

beginner: The most important time to keep watering steady is from flowering through when the fruit is filling out; big swings between dry and wet then make the tree drop flowers and fruit. A newly planted tree also needs careful, steady watering while it gets established.
seasoned: Even soil moisture matters most from bloom through fruit set and during fruit sizing; moisture swings in these windows trigger flower and fruit drop. Newly planted trees through their first establishment year are the other critical window, needing steady moisture to root in. beginner: Use limes soon after picking; they do not keep as long as lemons and do not like a very cold fridge. Keep them cool, and freeze the juice from any extras.
seasoned: Do not try to store limes like lemons. They are short-lived once picked and chilling-sensitive, so use them fresh, keep them only cool (about 50°F) not cold, and preserve a heavy summer pick as frozen juice and zest.
